COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (CNN) -- Sri Lanka President Mahinda Rajapaksa claimed Friday there was "a conspiracy with certain international forces" to belittle his government's military victories against Tamil Tiger rebels. Sri Lankan army troops have had there most decisive victories against the Tamil Tigers in recent weeks. The aim of these conspirators, he said in an address to the nation, "is to level unfounded charges against the army commander who works with greatest dedication to achieve these victories." He also used the address to formally announce the recapture of the northern town of Elephant Pass, the point at which mainland Sri Lanka links to the northern Jaffna peninsula. It had remained in rebel hands for over nine years. The recapture enable the government to use the A-9 highway linking the mainland to the peninsula to move troops and supplies. Until now it was done either by air or by sea. Rajapaksa's remarks came amid mounting attacks on the media. On Tuesday a group armed with rifles, pistols and grenades attacked the country's most popular privately owned television channel MTV. The main control room equipment costing more than $ 1.7 million was damaged. On Thursday, Lasantha Wickrematunga, chief editor of The Sunday Leader, a newspaper which had exposed corruption and criticized aspects of ongoing military operations, was shot dead. Earlier Friday, the leader of the main opposition United National Party (UNP), Ranil Wickremasinghe, accused military and security officials of the attacks, saying the government could not control them. "Armed forces members are shocked about these incidents. The armed forces says due to the activities of few intelligence sections, the reputation of the country is being ruined. That is the team which the government has no control of," he told parliament. Rajapaksa said there were efforts to belittle military victories "to turn the attention of the people to other directions." He said such "conspiracies arise when a country moves ahead without giving in to external pressures." He added "one must not mistake these conspiracies as being against me or my government. This is a conspiracy against the entire country by those who have been driven to fear due to the successes of our security forces." Meanwhile, fighting in northern Sri Lanka between government and rebel forces escalated on several fronts Friday, while Tamil Tiger rebels killed seven people in a roadside bombing. Three members of the Sri Lankan air force and four civilians died when rebels exploded a claymore landmine in the village of Morawewa, near the northeastern port city of Trincomalee, police said. The strategic port town is located about 240km (150 miles) north of the capital, Colombo. Friday's incident came as troops pursued their military campaign in the northern Wanni region to recapture remaining rebel strongholds, military sources said. Government troops were said to be meeting fierce resistance as they advanced on the Tamil stronghold of Mullaitivu and a naval blockade remained in the northeastern seas. The 25-year long civil war has left more than 65,000 people dead. The U.S. State Department has designated the Tamil Tigers a terrorist organization.

COLOMBO, Sri Lanka (CNN) — Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa said Friday that “certain international forces” were involved in a conspiracy to undermine his government’s military successes against the Tamil Tiger rebels.

In recent weeks, Sri Lankan army forces have achieved some of their most significant victories over the Tamil Tigers. In a national address, Rajapaksa said the purpose of the alleged plot was “to level unfounded charges against the army commander,” whom he described as working with great commitment to secure those victories.

During the same speech, he officially declared that government forces had retaken Elephant Pass, a northern town that connects mainland Sri Lanka with the Jaffna peninsula. The area had been under rebel control for more than nine years. Its recapture allows the government to use the A-9 highway to transport troops and supplies between the mainland and the peninsula, a route that had previously been replaced by air and sea transport.

Rajapaksa’s comments came as attacks on the media were increasing. On Tuesday, armed men carrying rifles, pistols and grenades assaulted MTV, the country’s most popular privately owned television station. Equipment in the main control room, worth more than $1.7 million, was damaged.

On Thursday, Lasantha Wickrematunga, editor-in-chief of The Sunday Leader, was shot and killed. His newspaper had reported on corruption and had criticized parts of the continuing military campaign.

Earlier Friday, Ranil Wickremasinghe, head of the main opposition United National Party, accused military and security officials of being responsible for the attacks, saying the government was unable to control them.

“Armed forces members are shocked about these incidents,” he told parliament. “The armed forces says due to the activities of few intelligence sections, the reputation of the country is being ruined. That is the team which the government has no control of.”

Rajapaksa said attempts were being made to diminish the army’s achievements “to turn the attention of the people to other directions.” He argued that such “conspiracies arise when a country moves ahead without giving in to external pressures.”

He added that people should not see the alleged plots as directed only at him or his administration. “This is a conspiracy against the entire country by those who have been driven to fear due to the successes of our security forces,” he said.

At the same time, combat between government troops and rebel fighters intensified on several fronts in northern Sri Lanka on Friday. Tamil Tiger rebels also killed seven people in a roadside bomb attack.

Police said three Sri Lankan air force personnel and four civilians were killed when rebels detonated a claymore mine in Morawewa, a village near the northeastern port city of Trincomalee. The strategically important port lies roughly 240 kilometers, or 150 miles, north of Colombo.

The bombing occurred as government forces continued their campaign in the northern Wanni region to seize the rebels’ remaining strongholds, according to military sources. Troops were reportedly facing strong resistance as they moved toward Mullaitivu, a Tamil Tiger stronghold, while a naval blockade continued in the northeastern seas.

Sri Lanka’s 25-year civil war has killed more than 65,000 people. The U.S. State Department has listed the Tamil Tigers as a terrorist organization.

outputs.L5:
Colombo is the vibrant commercial capital of Sri Lanka and one of the most fascinating cities in South Asia. Located on the island’s western coast, Colombo blends modern city life with a rich colonial history, colorful markets, religious landmarks, and oceanfront beauty.

As the largest city in Sri Lanka, Colombo is often the first stop for travelers arriving in the country. The city offers a unique mix of cultures, including Sinhalese, Tamil, Muslim, Burgher, and many others, all of which contribute to its food, architecture, festivals, and daily life. Visitors can explore historic sites such as the Colombo Fort area, the Old Parliament Building, and the Dutch Hospital precinct, which has been transformed into a popular dining and shopping destination.

One of Colombo’s most iconic places is Galle Face Green, a long seaside promenade where locals and tourists gather to enjoy the sunset, fly kites, and taste Sri Lankan street food. The city is also home to important religious sites, including the Gangaramaya Temple, one of the most famous Buddhist temples in Sri Lanka, as well as mosques, churches, and Hindu temples that reflect Colombo’s diverse identity.

For those interested in shopping and local life, Pettah Market is a must-visit. Its busy streets are filled with stalls selling spices, textiles, electronics, fruits, and countless everyday goods. Colombo also has modern shopping malls, luxury hotels, art galleries, and a growing café culture.

Food is another highlight of Colombo. From rice and curry to hoppers, kottu roti, fresh seafood, and tropical fruits, the city offers an unforgettable introduction to Sri Lankan cuisine. Whether dining in a fine restaurant or trying snacks from a street vendor, visitors can experience the bold flavors and warm hospitality for which Sri Lanka is known.

Colombo is more than just a gateway to Sri Lanka’s beaches, tea plantations, and ancient cities. It is a dynamic destination in its own right, where tradition and modernity meet by the Indian Ocean. For anyone traveling to Sri Lanka, Colombo offers an exciting first impression of the island’s culture, history, and charm.

**Rajapaksa says foreign forces trying to undermine Sri Lanka’s military gains**

**Colombo, Sri Lanka** — Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa has accused unnamed international forces of conspiring to undermine his government’s military campaign against the Tamil Tigers, as the army celebrates major battlefield gains including the recapture of the strategic Elephant Pass.

Speaking amid heightened tensions over the country’s long-running civil war, Rajapaksa said external actors were attempting to weaken public support for the military at a time when government forces say they are close to defeating the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE.

The comments came after the Sri Lankan military announced it had retaken Elephant Pass, a narrow causeway linking the Jaffna Peninsula with the rest of the island. The area had been held by the LTTE for years and was considered one of the rebels’ most important strongholds in the north.

Government officials described the recapture as a decisive victory in the campaign to dismantle the separatist movement, which has fought for decades to create an independent Tamil homeland in northern and eastern Sri Lanka.

But Rajapaksa’s remarks also come during a period of growing concern over attacks on journalists and media organizations critical of the government or its handling of the war.

In recent days, Sri Lanka has seen violence targeting the press, including attacks on media outlets and journalists. Press freedom groups and human rights organizations have warned that reporters face increasing intimidation as the conflict enters what the government describes as its final phase.

The government has denied any role in attacks on journalists and has said it is committed to investigating violence against the media. Officials have also argued that some criticism of the military campaign damages national security and benefits the LTTE.

The Tamil Tigers, listed as a terrorist organization by the United States, the European Union and others, have been blamed for suicide bombings, assassinations and attacks on civilians during the conflict. The group has also accused the government of abuses against Tamil civilians, allegations Colombo has denied.

Elephant Pass has long held symbolic and strategic importance. Its loss to the Tigers in 2000 was a major blow to the Sri Lankan military, while its recapture gives government forces greater control over access to Jaffna and further isolates remaining LTTE-held territory.

As the army advances deeper into rebel areas, aid agencies have expressed concern for civilians trapped in the fighting. The government says it is taking steps to protect noncombatants, while accusing the LTTE of using civilians as human shields.

Rajapaksa has framed the military offensive as a campaign to reunify the country and end terrorism. Critics, however, say the government’s wartime rhetoric has contributed to a climate in which dissent is treated as disloyalty.

With the LTTE under increasing pressure and the government declaring victory after victory, Sri Lanka remains sharply divided between national celebration over military gains and mounting concern over the cost to civilians, journalists and democratic freedoms.

counterfactuals.output:
**Sri Lankan Forces Press Tiger Rebels in North as Political Tensions Deepen After Editor’s Killing**

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka, January 2009** — Sri Lankan government forces have seized a string of key positions from the Tamil Tiger rebels in the island’s north, officials said, as President Mahinda Rajapaksa accused unnamed “conspirators” of trying to destabilize the country following the assassination of a prominent anti-government newspaper editor.

The military’s rapid advances mark one of the most decisive phases of Sri Lanka’s long civil war, now in its 26th year. Government troops, backed by artillery, air power and multiple infantry divisions, have pushed deep into territory once administered by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, tightening the noose around the rebels’ remaining strongholds in the northeastern Vanni region.

Earlier this month, the army captured **Kilinochchi**, the LTTE’s de facto political capital, in a major symbolic victory for Colombo. Days later, troops took control of **Elephant Pass**, the strategic gateway linking the Jaffna peninsula to the mainland, reversing one of the government’s most humiliating battlefield losses from earlier in the war. Military officials said soldiers were continuing operations toward the eastern coastal belt, where the Tigers are believed to be regrouping with thousands of civilians trapped in shrinking rebel-held areas.

The government has framed the offensive as the final stage of a campaign to defeat the LTTE, which has fought since 1983 for an independent Tamil homeland in the north and east. The war has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced hundreds of thousands more.

But as the battlefield shifted in the government’s favor, the country was shaken by the killing of **Lasantha Wickrematunga**, the outspoken editor of *The Sunday Leader*, who was shot by gunmen on motorcycles in a Colombo suburb on January 8. Wickrematunga, a fierce critic of Rajapaksa’s administration and of alleged corruption and abuses in the war effort, later died of his injuries in hospital.

His killing drew international condemnation and deepened fears among journalists and rights groups that dissenting voices are being silenced as the war reaches its climax. Wickrematunga had repeatedly said he was under threat, and his newspaper had published stories critical of senior government figures. Authorities promised an investigation, while denying any state involvement.

In an unusually charged response, President Rajapaksa suggested that the assassination was part of a broader plot to embarrass or undermine his government at a critical moment in the war. He accused shadowy forces of using the killing to damage Sri Lanka’s image abroad and distract from military victories against the LTTE.

Opposition leaders and media-rights advocates rejected that framing, saying the government must focus on finding the killers rather than invoking conspiracy claims. They said the murder raised urgent questions about impunity and the safety of journalists in a country where attacks on media workers have often gone unresolved.

Meanwhile, violence continued outside the northern war zone. Police and military officials said suspected Tamil Tiger rebels carried out a **roadside bombing near Trincomalee** in eastern Sri Lanka, targeting security forces in an area long contested by the LTTE. The blast underscored the rebels’ continued ability to strike beyond the shrinking front lines, even as they lose conventional territory in the north.

The LTTE has increasingly relied on mines, ambushes, suicide attacks and bombings as government troops have captured bases, supply routes and administrative centers. The rebels have not consistently commented on individual attacks, but the government routinely blames the group for roadside bombs and assaults on military and civilian targets.

Humanitarian agencies have warned that civilians trapped in the Vanni are facing severe shortages of food, medicine and shelter as fighting intensifies. The government says it is trying to create safe routes for civilians to leave rebel-held areas, while accusing the LTTE of using civilians as human shields. The Tigers deny those accusations and accuse the military of shelling populated areas.

Independent verification of battlefield claims remains difficult because journalists and aid workers face strict limits on access to the combat zone.

With Kilinochchi fallen, Elephant Pass retaken and rebel territory contracting rapidly, Sri Lanka appears to be entering a decisive and dangerous phase. The government says victory over the LTTE is now within reach. But the assassination of Wickrematunga, the president’s conspiracy allegations and continued insurgent attacks in the east suggest that even as the conventional war shifts in Colombo’s favor, Sri Lanka’s political and security crisis is far from over.

Independent verification of battlefield claims was not possible because journalists and most aid workers are barred from the front lines.

Tensions also rose after authorities blamed the LTTE for a claymore mine attack that targeted security forces. Claymore mines — directional explosives often detonated remotely — have been used frequently during Sri Lanka’s long civil war. Officials said the attack bore the hallmarks of the Tigers, though the rebels have in the past denied responsibility for attacks on civilians and some strikes attributed to them by the government.

The LTTE, which has fought since 1983 for an independent homeland for Sri Lanka’s ethnic Tamil minority, has suffered a series of battlefield setbacks as the military pushed deeper into rebel-held areas. The government has vowed to destroy the group militarily, rejecting renewed calls for negotiations unless the Tigers lay down their arms.

Human rights groups and foreign governments have expressed concern about civilian casualties, disappearances and restrictions on humanitarian access in the conflict zone. Colombo has dismissed much of the criticism as biased, saying its forces are conducting operations with care and accusing the rebels of using civilians as shields.

The intensifying campaign in the Wanni has raised fears of a worsening humanitarian crisis, with tens of thousands of civilians believed to be trapped or displaced by the fighting. Aid agencies have warned that access to food, medicine and shelter remains limited as the front lines shift.

Sri Lanka’s civil war has killed tens of thousands of people over more than two decades and remains one of Asia’s longest-running separatist conflicts.
